CC6010 · Digital Investigation and E-Discovery · Week 3 · E-Discovery Practical

Email E-Discovery
with Autopsy

A guided e-discovery workshop using the NPS 2010 Emails E01 test image. You will process collected digital evidence, identify potentially relevant email-related ESI, review keyword hits, trace them back to their source files, and compare information stored in plain, encoded, compressed and embedded content.

Tool: Autopsy 4.23.1
Evidence: nps-2010-emails.E01
Focus: Identification · Processing · Review
Duration: ~60–75 minutes
🧠 WHAT ARE WE DOING?

This workshop focuses on the e-discovery side of CC6010. The evidence has already been collected for you as an E01 image. Your task is to use Autopsy to identify, process and review potentially relevant email-related electronically stored information (ESI).

You are not investigating email transmission or attribution in this practical. That would involve message headers, mail-server logs and routing evidence. Here, the question is whether relevant email-related information can be located within a collected body of digital evidence and reliably traced back to its source.

Identification
Locate potentially relevant email-related ESI within the collected evidence.
Processing
Use Autopsy to extract and index searchable content from files, archives and embedded objects.
Review
Examine keyword hits and trace each result back to its parent or extracted source.
Relevance
Decide what each result contributes to the matter and avoid treating every hit as a separate relevant item.
💡 Important distinction

The test image contains 30 target email addresses, but keyword-result counts can be higher because a value may appear in both a parent object and an extracted child object. Treat hits and unique artefacts as different things.

📁 CASE BRIEFING
// Internal e-discovery review · Collected source: workstation image · Review tool: Autopsy

An organisation is conducting an internal review and has collected a forensic image of a workstation that may contain email-related information relevant to the matter.

The information may not be stored in obvious locations. Relevant email addresses could exist in ordinary documents, compressed archives, nested files, embedded objects or text stored using different character encodings.

The collected evidence has been provided as nps-2010-emails.E01.

Your role is to use Autopsy to identify potentially relevant ESI, process the collected content, review the resulting keyword hits, trace each hit back to its source, and determine what should be retained for further review.

🔎 What are we actually looking for?

You are not trying to prove who sent or received an email. This practical is about finding and reviewing email-related ESI inside collected digital evidence.

Your central e-discovery question is:

What potentially relevant email-related ESI exists within the collected evidence, where is it located, and can it be reliably traced back to its source?

Identify
Find email-address strings that may be relevant to the review.
Process
Expose searchable content from encoded, compressed, nested and embedded data.
Review
Examine each hit in context and trace it to its source file or extracted object.
Assess relevance
Decide whether a hit is distinct, duplicated, or potentially relevant for further review.
🎯 Review questions
  • What email-related ESI can you identify?
  • Where is each item stored?
  • Can Autopsy expose relevant content from compressed, nested, embedded and UTF-16 data?
  • Can each keyword hit be traced back to a parent or extracted source?
  • Are any results duplicates of the same underlying information?
  • Which findings would you retain for further review, and why?
💬 How to think like an e-discovery reviewer

For every result, ask: What was found? Where did it come from? Is it a distinct item? Is it potentially relevant to the matter?

PART 1 — LOAD THE COLLECTED EVIDENCE

⏱ ~10 minutes

Step 1
Create a new Autopsy case

Open Autopsy and create a new case for the workshop. Use a clear case name such as CC6010_Week3_Email_Artifacts.

Step 2
Add the forensic image as a data source

Select Add Data Source and choose the disk-image/image-file option. Browse to nps-2010-emails.E01 and continue.

What to check
  • The file name shown by Autopsy is nps-2010-emails.E01.
  • Autopsy recognises it as an image data source.
  • Do not begin interpreting findings before ingest has completed.
PART 2 — PROCESS THE ESI

⏱ ~10 minutes

Step 3
Enable Keyword Search

During ingest configuration, enable Keyword Search. Make sure the Email Addresses keyword list is included.

💡 What Autopsy is doing

The module searches extracted text for patterns that match email-address structures. The hit is useful, but it still needs to be tied back to its source file and interpreted in context.

Step 4
Allow ingest to finish

Wait until Autopsy finishes processing the image. Then move to the results tree on the left side of the interface.

PART 3 — REVIEW THE EMAIL-RELATED ESI

⏱ ~10 minutes

Step 5
Open the keyword hits

Navigate to:

Analysis Results → Keyword Hits → Email Addresses

Autopsy should display the recovered email-address hits. Select individual entries and use the lower Extracted Text pane to validate what was recovered.

🧠 Pause and think

Why can the result count be larger than the number of distinct target email addresses? Do not assume that every hit represents a different artefact.

⚑ FINDING 1 — GZIP-COMPRESSED CONTENT
Your task
  • Locate the email-address hit associated with GZIP content.
  • Identify the extracted source file shown by Autopsy.
  • Use the Extracted Text pane to verify the recovered string.
  • Write one sentence explaining why this matters in a forensic investigation.
Need a hint / check your result after attempting?

Look for email_in_gzip@gzipfile.com. The supplied analysis traced it to myfilegzip.txt.

⚑ FINDING 2 — NESTED GZIP CONTENT
Your task
  • Find the email artefact that originated from content compressed more than once.
  • Trace it to the extracted source file.
  • Explain why a simple file-system review could miss evidence like this.
Need a hint / check your result after attempting?

Look for email_in_gzip_gzip@gzipfile.com. The supplied analysis traced it to myfilegzip2.txt.

⚑ FINDING 3 — EMBEDDED DOCUMENT OBJECT
Your task
  • Locate an email address associated with an embedded document object.
  • Compare the parent/source document with the extracted child object.
  • Explain why examining only the parent filename would be insufficient.
Need a hint / check your result after attempting?

The supplied analysis found doc_within_doc@document.com in parent doc_within_doc.doc, with an extracted object shown as image_0.emf.

⚑ FINDING 4 — UTF-16 ENCODED TEXT
Your task
  • Locate an address stored using UTF-16 encoding.
  • Record its source file.
  • Explain why forensic searches should account for different character encodings.
Need a hint / check your result after attempting?

The supplied analysis identified plain_utf16@textedit.com in document3.txt.

📋 REVIEW RECORD — WHAT TO SUBMIT / DISCUSS

For each of your four findings, record the review result in a short, structured way. Focus on source, relevance and duplication rather than writing a long essay.

FindingRecovered ESISource / extracted fileReview significanceLimitation
GZIPComplete in classComplete in classExplain what Autopsy recoveredA keyword hit does not prove an email was sent
Nested GZIPComplete in classComplete in classExplain why nested content mattersInterpret in context
Embedded objectComplete in classComplete in classExplain parent/child relationshipDo not rely on parent filename alone
UTF-16Complete in classComplete in classExplain encoding relevanceSearch configuration affects what is found
⚠️ Forensic language

Finding an email address inside a file supports the statement that the string was present in the examined evidence. It does not, by itself, prove that an email was sent, received, read, or authored by a particular person.

🧩 WHAT DID WE LEARN?
1 · Ingest first
A forensic image must be processed before analysis results can be interpreted.
2 · Search is only the start
A keyword hit must be traced to its source or extracted object.
3 · Evidence can be hidden by structure
Compression, nested containers and embedded objects can conceal relevant searchable content.
4 · Encoding matters
A search that ignores alternate encodings may miss relevant strings.
✓ Core Week 3 takeaway

A good e-discovery review result is not simply “Autopsy found an email address.” It records what was identified, where it came from, whether it is distinct or duplicated, and why it may be relevant for further review.

RESULT

🧾 E-DISCOVERY REVIEW CONCLUSION

At the end of the workshop, your conclusion should summarise what the review process identified and why the processing stage mattered.

✓ Example conclusion structure

The review identified potentially relevant email-related ESI across multiple storage formats, including encoded text, compressed content, nested archives and embedded document objects. Autopsy processing exposed content that was not immediately visible and allowed the reviewer to trace keyword hits back to their source files or extracted objects. Duplicate hits were interpreted in context rather than treated automatically as separate relevant items.

⚠️ Scope of this practical

This workshop focuses on identification, processing and review of ESI. It does not establish who sent or received an email, because message headers, mail-server logs and routing evidence are outside the scope of this exercise.
